编制 Round 25 提审准备 checklist，检查论文当前状态的各项准备工作。

## 背景
目标：EMNLP 2026 ARR May（DDL 2026-05-25）。Round 24 得分 3.25/5（borderline），冲 Main Conference 4.0。论文改动包括 R24 全部修复 + scaling 数据 + 新 appendix。需要确认提审前所有 checklist 项都通过。

EMNLP 2026 限制：long paper 正文 8 页，references 不限，limitations 和 ethical considerations 不计入页数（前提是不含过多额外内容）。

## 具体步骤

### 1. 论文编译状态
SSH 到有论文源码的服务器（先检查本地 artifacts 目录是否有 .tex 文件）：
- 检查 `/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_1/projects/struct_self_consist_ie/artifacts/` 下是否有完整论文 tex
- 或检查项目的 paper 目录结构
- 读取 `read_project_file(project="struct_self_consist_ie", file="paper_framing.md")` 了解论文结构

### 2. 编制 Checklist（逐项列出状态）

**格式与页数**
- [ ] 正文 ≤ 8 页（不含 references, limitations, ethics）
- [ ] 使用正确的 ARR/EMNLP 模板
- [ ] 匿名化（无作者信息、无 "our previous work" 等泄露）

**内容完整性**
- [ ] Abstract 反映最新实验结果
- [ ] 所有 Table/Figure 引用完整（无 "??" 或 "Table ??"）
- [ ] 所有 \ref, \cite 解析成功
- [ ] Scaling section (§5.5) 数据完整（需要 7B/14B/32B 数据——标记为 PENDING）
- [ ] Appendix 完整性（列出所有 appendix section，标记哪些有数据哪些待填）

**数值一致性**
- [ ] 正文中引用的数值与 Table 中一致
- [ ] Abstract 中的数值与正文一致
- [ ] 已关闭的数值审计项（列出 report.md 中的审计清单）

**排版质量**
- [ ] Overfull hbox 数量（编译 log 中的 warning 数）
- [ ] 图表清晰度、字体大小
- [ ] References 格式一致

**提交材料**
- [ ] Response letter / revision summary（如果 ARR 要求）
- [ ] Supplementary materials / code / data availability statement
- [ ] Reproducibility checklist（ARR 标准）

### 3. 读取最新论文 tex 文件
在 artifacts 目录中搜索 .tex 文件，读取 main tex 文件检查：
- 页数（通过 section 结构估算）
- 是否有 "??" 占位符
- overfull hbox（如果有编译 log）

## 输出
将 checklist 写入本地文件：
`/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_1/projects/struct_self_consist_ie/artifacts/round25_submission_checklist.md`

每项标注 ✅ PASS / ⚠️ WARN / ❌ FAIL / ⏳ PENDING，附具体说明。

注册 artifact: `register_artifact(project="struct_self_consist_ie", name="round25_submission_checklist", path="artifacts/round25_submission_checklist.md", type="checklist")`

ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Within fixed dataset-model settings, degeneracy causally modulates LP effectiveness (SciERC epoch ablation: −1.18/+0.74/+0.99pp at 3/5/10 epochs; per-entity-type within Few-NERD ρ=−0.881). But across datasets, degeneracy alone does NOT predict LP selection direction (23-point cross-configuration ρ=0.052, p=0.81).
- **LP-quality alignment as primary predictor**: LP must track entity-level F1 within instances. Few-NERD within-instance ρ(LP,F1) ≈ 0.5-0.66 → LP selection +1.36pp (p<0.05). SciERC ρ(LP,F1) ≈ 0.18-0.24 → LP fails despite similar degeneracy (17.8% vs 13.8%). This is the primary determinant of LP selection success across datasets.
- **Structural signals (SJ/FK/EM/VC)**: universally fail regardless — instance-level aggregates cannot rank candidates by construction.
- **Multi-causal diagnosis (D154)**: (1) degeneracy modulates headroom within settings; (2) LP-quality alignment determines cross-dataset selection success; (3) LoRA rank=8 reduces degeneracy (7.2% vs 17.8%) AND improves LP spread (0.057 vs 0.041 nats) but SciERC's weak LP-F1 alignment (ρ~0.24) still prevents selection success → LP alignment is the binding constraint, degeneracy is a within-setting modulator.

The framing is NOT "selection fails" (pure negative) but "we characterize WHEN LP works (strong LP-F1 alignment), WHY it fails elsewhere (weak alignment + compression), and WHAT distinguishes LP from structural signals" (empirical characterization with diagnostic implications).

**Three-layer argument + Capability-diversity tension**:
- Layer A (design property, noted not discovered): 4/5 signals are instance-level aggregates → cannot rank candidates by construction. This is a conceptual clarification — the "methodological premise" — not an empirical finding.
- Layer B (empirical — instance degeneracy): 21-58% of instances produce identical F1 across all N samples, eliminating selection headroom. Within-instance ρ=0.524 (SciERC) and 0.994 (CoNLL) — signals ARE correlated within instances, but degeneracy makes this irrelevant. Non-degenerate instances show MBR closing 23-41% of oracle gap. Selection recovers T=1.0 sampling degradation (LP 0.647 vs Random 0.610, +3.7pp) but only matches T=0 greedy (0.645 macro) at 8× inference cost — zero marginal gain.
- Layer C (empirical — LP-quality alignment, revised D123): LP selection requires adequate within-instance correlation with task quality. Few-NERD ρ(LP,F1)≈0.5-0.66 → selection succeeds (+1.36pp). SciERC ρ(LP,F1)≈0.18-0.24 → selection fails even when LP range is adequate (rank=8: 0.057 nats). LP compression (median range 0.041 nats on SciERC full-rank) is a contributing factor but NOT the sole explanation — rank=8 expands LP range to 0.057 yet still fails. Entity-token LP shows 4× variance but WORSE selection (-2.0pp). Free-form ablation confirms compression is model/task intrinsic for NER (std ratio 0.97).
- **Capability-diversity tension** (unifying insight, D111): Model capability → output convergence → instance degeneracy → vanishing selection headroom. Evidence: CoNLL (91% F1) → 58% degeneracy, SciERC (66% F1) → 21%, WNUT (48% F1) → ~0%. Scale dimension: 8B → 21% degen vs 4B → 10.4% on SciERC. This is NOT an "artifact" — it is a **consequence of capability**, a structural inevitability. The better the model, the less test-time scaling can help via unsupervised selection.

**Distinction from MBR literature**: Eikema et al.'s MBR failure = utility function misalignment. Our failure = utility IS aligned (within-instance ρ=0.524) but headroom eliminated by degeneracy — qualitatively novel mechanism.

**Key evidence (score compression)**:
- Non-tied subset (40%): logprob selection +2.9pp vs greedy (p=0.01), within-instance ρ: 0.08→0.39
- Full set: logprob +0.6pp, bootstrap p=0.39, Cohen's d=0.038 (negligible), 95% CI [-3.0, +4.2]pp
- Oracle headroom: NER +13pp, RE +18pp → information exists but signals can't access it

**Key evidence (free-form ablation)** [DONE — exp_freeform_ablation, NEGATIVE]:
- LP distribution: constrained std=0.0206, free-form std=0.0199 (ratio 0.97, virtually unchanged)
- Tied fraction: 59.7% → 57.7% (-2.0pp, negligible)
- NER selection: +0.59pp → +0.18pp (both negligible vs greedy)
- RE selection: -0.68pp → +1.69pp (flipped positive — secondary finding)
- NER VC rho: 0.379 → 0.409 (slight QE improvement, selection still fails)
- Parse rate: 99.95% (fine-tuned model retains JSON format without grammar)
- **Conclusion**: Score compression is model/task intrinsic. The gap is universal.

**Key evidence (scale ablation)** [DONE — 2×2 matrix: {CoNLL, SciERC} × {Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B}]:
- CoNLL NER: 4B greedy_f1=0.9234 (>8B 0.9123, +1.11pp), SJ_ρ=0.4217 (≈8B 0.4357, −1.4pp), FK_ρ=0.4181 (>8B 0.3998, +1.83pp)
- SciERC NER: 4B SJ_ρ=0.4221 (>8B 0.3825, +3.96pp), FK_ρ=0.3258 (>8B 0.2590, +6.68pp)
- SciERC RE: 4B SJ_ρ=0.2673 (>8B 0.2441, +2.32pp), FK_ρ=0.3593 (>8B 0.2782, +8.11pp); struct>surface ✗ at both scales
- **Conclusion**: Correlation strength maintained or improved at 4B across all 4 cells. The gap originates from within-instance signal misalignment, not model capacity. Task difficulty (SciERC RE zero-F1 rate) remains the primary driver, consistent across scales.
- CoNLL 4B headroom: 1.70pp (vs 8B 4.20pp) → MARGINAL for selection power, but QE correlations robust
- SciERC RE 4B: 47.6% zero-F1, RE LP_ρ_cond=0.1135 (p=0.074, n.s.) → confirms binary dominance at 4B
- **4B selection results** (correlation-selection gap at 4B):
  - CoNLL NER 4B (n=2756): SJ +0.07pp, FK +0.03pp, LP +0.09pp vs greedy 0.9213. All ≤0.1pp — MARGINAL (headroom 1.70pp)
  - SciERC NER 4B (n=529): SJ **-1.49pp**, FK -1.56pp, LP -2.23pp vs greedy 0.6622. Oracle 0.7925 (+13.02pp). **All signals WORSE than greedy despite 13pp oracle headroom — gap confirmed at 4B**
  - SciERC NER 4B gap demonstration: SJ-FK ρ gap = +0.096 (strong correlation advantage), SJ-FK selection F1 gap = +0.0007 (zero selection advantage) → correlation-selection gap quantified at 4B
- **n_samples confound control**: Qwen3-8B n=8 data exists as control. CoNLL SJ: n8 ρ=0.4389 → n16 ρ=0.4496 (Δ=0.011, CI crosses zero). SciERC SJ: n8→n16 Δ=0.066, CI=[0.004, 0.128] weak effect. n_samples not a confound for 4B-8B comparison.
- **Paper framing**: "Scale ablation shows the gap is not an artifact of a particular model size; correlation strength is maintained at 4B, confirming that the gap originates from within-instance signal misalignment rather than model capacity."

**exp-019 supervised verifier**: IN PROGRESS (D116 Dream feedback — all 3 tiers flagged as critical gap). Simplified to logistic regression on 5 signals (scikit-learn, CPU, ~30min). If supervised verifier partially closes oracle gap → proves gap IS closable, signals carry information but unsupervised heuristics are too weak. Grounds the "what would be needed" part of Contribution B.

QE correlation preserved (VC ρ=0.394, SJ ρ=0.365). **Key insight**: Reducing degeneracy is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT — signals themselves lack the discriminative power to exploit increased headroom. Strengthens multi-causal argument and points to trained verifiers as the path forward. Dream 三档公认最强实验。

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks across fine-tuned 4B\textendash 8B and zero-shot 72B models.
All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL-2003, area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
For instance-level selection, log-probability (LP) succeeds only where LP-quality alignment is strong, and gains are absent elsewhere despite large oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
We identify three qualitative factors: instance degeneracy, oracle headroom, and LP-quality alignment; the gap persists at 72B zero-shot scale, confirming it is a structural property of the task rather than a fine-tuning artifact.
The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level \textit{construction}, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation improves F1 by $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC under fine-tuning (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$). Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment.
\end{abstract}

5	\label{sec:setup}

7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, each serving a distinct role.

12	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 51\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary where model capability is insufficient.
13	
14	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
15	\textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are LoRA fine-tuned using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} (training details in Appendix~\ref{app:training}; Few-NERD uses 3 epochs vs.\ 5 for others due to earlier convergence; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
16	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary) with vLLM constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}, with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).

19	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}

45	\paragraph{Signal rankings are difficulty-dependent.}
46	On SciERC (medium difficulty), structural signals lead (VC $\rho{=}0.379$, SJ $0.360$) over LP ($0.205$); bootstrap CIs confirm the gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
47	On CoNLL (single-sample F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads both $\rho$ and AUROC ($0.816$).
48	At the signal-collapse boundary (WNUT-17, macro F1${\approx}$42\%), full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary (VC $\rho{=}0.724$ at $N{=}16$, but conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); LP shows the reverse (conditional $\rho{=}0.350$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}).

51	%% ============================================================
52	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
53	\label{sec:selection_gap}
54	
55	Four of five signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input by construction (\S\ref{sec:formulation}); they can estimate quality across instances but cannot rank candidates within an instance.
56	The empirical question is whether LP, the sole per-sample signal, can exploit its candidate-discriminative nature for selection.
57	LP selection effectiveness is primarily determined by LP-quality alignment rather than degeneracy level (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
58	Cross-instance $\rho$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}) is attenuated by varying instance difficulty; within-instance $\rho$ directly measures whether LP discriminates candidates for a fixed input, making it the relevant predictor of selection success.
59

Non-tied subset in \S\ref{sec:discussion}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}. $^\dagger$Instance-level signals assign one score per input; per-sample ranking $p$-values are undefined.}

89	\caption{The correlation-selection gap on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Bars: quality estimation $\rho$ (seed 42); line with error bars: $\Delta$F1 vs.\ greedy (3-seed mean, seeds 42/123/456). Despite $\rho$ up to 0.38, no signal significantly outperforms greedy (all $p{>}0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}). Dashed green: oracle upper bound ($+13.0$~pp); dotted gray: random baseline.}
90	\label{fig:selection_gap}
91	\end{figure}
92	
93	Instance-level signals assign identical QE scores to all candidates; MBR conversion does not improve over greedy on the primary test bed (Table~\ref{tab:selection}; Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
94	Instance-level signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} is best.
95	
96	\paragraph{LP: the sole per-sample signal also fails.}
97	On SciERC ($n{=}529$, 2-seed sign tests\footnote{MDE${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power ($n{=}529$); Few-NERD ($n{=}32{,}565$; MDE${\approx}$0.22~pp) provides the definitive test.}), the oracle (0.775) reveals 13.0~pp of headroom, but LP achieves $+0.2$~pp ($p{=}0.29$), below the MDE (${\approx}$1.5~pp); selection effects below this threshold cannot be reliably detected.
98	The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}); under stringent TOST anchors, some configurations show significant \textit{degradation} (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
99	Few-NERD provides the definitive contrast: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp ($p{<}0.001$) at low degeneracy (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}), while structural signals still degrade selection.
100	
101	\paragraph{Qualitative factors governing selection effectiveness.}
102	Three factors shape LP selection gains: (1)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (SciERC 17.8\%, CoNLL 61.7\%; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}); (2)~\textit{oracle headroom} (CoNLL ${\approx}4$\,pp vs.\ SciERC 13.0\,pp); (3)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (Few-NERD $\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$ vs.\ SciERC $\rho{\approx}0.26$).
103	The pattern matches observations: Few-NERD (low degeneracy, strong alignment) yields $+1.39$\,pp; SciERC (weak alignment) $+0.04{\pm}0.48$\,pp (3-seed; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}); CoNLL (high degeneracy) none; WNUT-17 shows reversed LP ($\rho{=}{-}0.446$) yet QE remains effective (VC $\rho{=}0.724$, $N{=}16$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
104	The factors do not combine into a predictive model ($R^2{<}0$, 23 configurations) but each is supported by controlled ablations (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
105	
106	%% ============================================================
107	\subsection{Cross-Dataset Contrast: Few-NERD}
108	\label{sec:fewnerd}
109

128	Few-NERD (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}) confirms LP selection at low degeneracy ($+1.39$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; structural signals degrade: VC $-1.79$, SJ $-2.14$~pp), with LP 50$\times$ more seed-stable ($\sigma{=}0.04$ vs.\ SJ $2.02$~pp), generalizing to LLaMA (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}). Training convergence modulates degeneracy (5-epoch: $31$\%, halving LP gains; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
129	
130	\paragraph{Degeneracy alone does not predict LP direction.}
131	Across 23 configurations, degeneracy does not predict LP gain ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$; Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy_scatter}), though it causally modulates LP within fixed settings ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}). Cross-dataset prediction requires LP signal quality (Appendix~\ref{app:conditional_decomp}).

137	\label{fig:degeneracy_scatter}
138	\end{figure}

140	Structural signals remain negative regardless of sample budget; $N$-scaling analyses are in Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}.
141	
142	%% ============================================================
143	\subsection{Robustness}
144	\label{sec:robustness_main}
145	
146	Consistency signals are robust across $T{\in}\{0.7, 1.0\}$ with sublinear $N$-scaling gains (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}); signal rankings are stable across seeds ($W{=}1.0$; Table~\ref{tab:ranking-stability}). NER calibration is reasonable (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}).
147	
148	\begin{table}[t]
149	\centering
150	\small
151	\caption{Scale ablation: 8B vs.\ 4B QE $\rho$ ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seed 42). RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.}
152	\label{tab:scale_ablation}
153	\begin{tabular}{@{}ll cc r@{}}
154	\toprule
155	& & \textbf{8B} & \textbf{4B} & $\Delta$ \\
156	\midrule
157	CoNLL & SJ & .436 & .422 & $-$.014 \\
158	      & FK & .400 & .418 & $+$.018 \\
159	SciERC & SJ & .360 & .422 & $+$.062 \\
160	       & FK & .267 & .326 & $+$.059 \\
161	\bottomrule
162	\end{tabular}
163	\end{table}
164	
165	\paragraph{Scale robustness.}
166	With Qwen3-4B (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), QE is comparable (mean $|\Delta\rho|{=}0.042$), yet selection remains below greedy despite 13.0~pp headroom. Task difficulty is a stronger predictor than model scale within the 3B--8B range (Appendix~\ref{app:llama3b}).
167	Degeneracy scales with capability: 8B shows 17.8\% vs.\ 4B's 10.4\% on SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
168	
169	\paragraph{Controlled ablations.}
170	LoRA rank${=}8$ (vs.\ 32) lowers degeneracy to 7.2\% but LP remains below greedy ($\rho{\approx}0.24$), confirming low degeneracy and adequate alignment are independently necessary ($T{=}1.2$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
171	Supervised classifiers, a DeBERTa verifier, and hidden state probes all fail to close the gap (Appendix~\ref{app:supervised_combination}, \ref{app:hidden_probe}); the bottleneck extends to model-internal representations.
172	
173	%% ============================================================
174	\subsection{Scaling Behavior}
175	\label{sec:scaling}
176	
177	We evaluate Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct in a zero-shot setting to test whether the gap persists at larger scale without fine-tuning.
178	
179	\begin{table}[t]
180	\centering
181	\small
182	\caption{Fine-tuned 8B vs.\ zero-shot 72B ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Hdr.\ = oracle $-$ greedy (pp). Degen.: instance degeneracy (\%). $^\dagger$Not computed for this configuration.}
183	\label{tab:scale_comparison}
184	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
185	\begin{tabular}{@{}llccccccc@{}}
186	\toprule
187	Dataset & Regime & Greedy & Hdr. & Degen. & VC & SJ & FK & LP \\
188	\midrule
189	SciERC & 8B FT  & .644 & 13.0 & 17.8 & .379 & .360 & .267 & .205 \\
190	       & 72B ZS & .399 & 15.0 & 21.0 & .277 & .217 & .227 & .081 \\
191	\midrule
192	Few-NERD & 8B FT & .748 & 12.4 & 13.0 & .386 & .300 & .313 & .220 \\
193	         & 72B ZS & .628 & ---$^\dagger$ & 46.2 & .416 & .345 & ---$^\dagger$ & .119 \\
194	\midrule
195	CoNLL  & 8B FT  & .908 & ${\approx}$4 & 61.7 & .424 & .436 & .400 & .302 \\
196	       & 72B ZS & .712 & 5.3 & 67.7 & .297 & .304 & .302 & $-$.002 \\
197	\bottomrule
198	\end{tabular}}
199	\end{table}
200	
201	LP $\rho$ drops without fine-tuning (Table~\ref{tab:scale_comparison}) and LP selection fails on all datasets. Structural signals generalize (Few-NERD VC $\rho{=}0.416$). Degeneracy increases (Few-NERD: $46.2$\% vs.\ $13.0$\%; CoNLL: $67.7$\% vs.\ $61.7$\%); this comparison simultaneously varies model family, regime, and quantization, so individual effects cannot be disentangled.
202	LP-weighted construction yields $+1.53$\,pp on SciERC 72B ZS ($p{=}0.008$, CI [$+0.25$, $+2.82$]), recovering $10.2$\% of headroom. Construction fails on Few-NERD ($-0.20$\,pp) and CoNLL ($-0.37$\,pp) where degeneracy exceeds $46$\%---consistent with FT-regime degeneracy gating.
203	
204	\paragraph{Few-shot demonstrations improve QE but not construction.}
205	Adding 3-shot demonstrations to 72B improves greedy on SciERC and CoNLL ($+3.3$--$6.2$\,pp) but not Few-NERD ($-0.9$\,pp), and strengthens structural QE (CoNLL SJ $\rho$ $.304{\to}.442$, LP $-.002{\to}.106$). Yet construction is ineffective across all three datasets (SciERC $-0.08$\,pp, CoNLL $+0.03$\,pp, Few-NERD $+0.02$\,pp; all n.s.). On SciERC, this failure despite low degeneracy shows the bottleneck is regime-dependent (the mechanism is not simple error correlation; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}); on Few-NERD, high FS degeneracy ($45.2$\%) places it in the expected failure regime.
206	
207	The capability--diversity tradeoff is consistent across available evidence: epoch ablations (5-epoch training triples degeneracy; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}) and cross-family comparisons (Qwen3-8B FT 13.0\%, $+1.40$\,pp vs.\ Qwen2.5-72B ZS 46.2\%, $-0.20$\,pp) both show higher capability compressing the improvability window.
208

211	
212	%% ============================================================
213	\subsection{Prescriptive Results}
214	\label{sec:prescriptive}
215	
216	Since instance-level selection fails, we present two approaches that extract value from multi-sample generation without sample ranking.
217	
218	\paragraph{Entity-level construction.}
219	Rather than selecting one complete output, we aggregate entities across samples, retaining those exceeding $\theta{=}2/N$, with LP-weighted or uniform scoring ($\theta$ stable in $[0.15, 0.35]$; Appendix~\ref{app:theta_sweep}). In zero-shot, uniform voting degrades due to noise entities; LP-weighting is necessary (SciERC $+1.5$\,pp; \S\ref{sec:scaling}).
220	
221	\begin{table}[t]
222	\centering
223	\small
224	\caption{Entity construction vs.\ greedy ($\Delta$ macro F1; $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B, multi-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$). $\theta{=}2/N$. $p$: paired bootstrap vs.\ greedy. Best in \textbf{bold}. $^\ddagger$LP-weighted not computed; uniform only.}
225	\label{tab:entity_construction}
226	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
227	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
228	\toprule
229	Dataset & Wt. & Greedy & Constr. & $\Delta$ & $p$ \\
230	\midrule
231	SciERC & LP & $.646{\pm}.002$ & $\mathbf{.656{\pm}.003}$ & $+1.02{\pm}0.49$\,pp & .004 \\
232	       & Unif. & $.646{\pm}.002$ & $.653{\pm}.006$ & $+0.74{\pm}0.71$\,pp & .023 \\
233	\addlinespace
234	Few-NERD & LP & $.748$ & $\mathbf{.762{\pm}.005}$ & $+1.40{\pm}0.51$\,pp & ${<}.001$ \\
235	         & Unif. & $.748$ & $.756{\pm}.006$ & $+0.74{\pm}0.58$\,pp & .003 \\
236	\addlinespace
237	CoNLL$^\ddagger$ & Unif. & .908 & .904 & $-0.39$\,pp & n.s. \\
238	\bottomrule
239	\end{tabular}}
240	\end{table}
241	
242	LP-weighted construction improves on Few-NERD ($+1.40{\pm}0.51$\,pp, $p{<}0.001$) and SciERC ($+1.02{\pm}0.49$\,pp, $p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}), positive across all 7 seed-dataset combinations, recovering 8--11\% of oracle headroom. CoNLL shows no gain ($-0.39$\,pp), consistent with high degeneracy. The mechanism is recall-driven ($N$-scaling in Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
243	
244	\paragraph{LP-alignment gating (preliminary diagnostic).}
245	Construction and LP selection are complementary: construction dominates on SciERC ($+1.02$\,pp vs.\ LP n.s.; $\rho{\approx}0.2$), while Few-NERD favors both ($+1.40$ vs.\ $+1.39$\,pp; $\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$).
246	We estimate degeneracy-adjusted $\rho_{\text{adj}}$ on 50 held-out instances: Few-NERD $0.516$ [0.459, 0.759], SciERC $0.167$, CoNLL $0.065$, WNUT-17 ${\approx}0$.
247	A three-way protocol ($\rho_{\text{adj}} \geq 0.3$: LP selection; $<0.3$ with positive construction: construction; else: greedy) routes Few-NERD to LP ($+1.39$\,pp) and the rest to greedy, stable across $\tau{\in}[0.2, 0.4]$.
248	
249	\paragraph{Selective prediction.}
250	Orthogonal to construction, QE signals support selective prediction: at 80\% coverage, filtering low-confidence instances yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (AUPRC 0.70--0.92; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
251	
252	\phantomsection\label{sec:selection_results}

29	\section{Robustness Analysis}\label{app:robustness}
30	
31	We exclude instances with empty gold annotations from all correlation analyses (CoNLL: 697/3{,}453 instances, 20.2\%; SciERC: 22/551, 4.0\%).
32	For these instances, F1 is trivially zero regardless of prediction quality, and consistency signals reflect agreement on the empty set rather than extraction quality. Including them inflates or deflates Spearman $\rho$ depending on signal behavior at the boundary.
33

Bottom: transfer across model families (both 8B) (LLaMA CoNLL $N{=}16$, 3-seed mean $\pm\sigma$). $^\dagger$Mean over 3 seeds ($\sigma{=}0.013$; individual: 0.398, 0.423, 0.410). $\sigma$ computed as sample standard deviation.}

70	\caption{Temperature robustness on SciERC ($N{=}8$). Top: NER; bottom: RE. SJ maintains stable $\rho$ across $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$, while FK shows mixed sensitivity. LP shows the largest NER temperature effect ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.044$); RE $T{=}0.7$ LP data unavailable.}
71	\label{fig:temperature_robustness}
72	\end{figure}
73	
74	\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
75	SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.364 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.004.
76	FK NER $\rho$ drops by 0.022, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
77	LP exhibits the largest temperature effect on NER ($\rho{=}0.249$ at $T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $0.205$ at $T{=}1.0$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.044$), consistent with lower temperature concentrating probability mass and improving LP's discriminative power for quality estimation; RE $T{=}0.7$ LP data is not available.
78	Across all comparisons, the signal hierarchy is preserved at both temperatures on NER (SJ${>}$FK${>}$LP at $T{=}0.7$: $0.364{>}0.289{>}0.249$; at $T{=}1.0$: $0.360{>}0.267{>}0.205$).
79	
80	\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (Soft Jaccard, voting confidence, Fleiss' $\kappa$, exact match) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Three factors qualitatively shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy} (13\textendash 68\% across our benchmarks) compresses the candidate space; (b)~\textit{oracle headroom} bounds the achievable gain; (c)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can discriminate candidates in non-degenerate instances (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
Our diagnosis is complementary to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap and its mitigation. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably estimate instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all samples from the same input, so best-of-$N$ selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction aggregates entities across samples via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$), bypassing the selection bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, multi-seed mean; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity across 4B\textendash 8B fine-tuned and 72B zero-shot regimes.
An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
The three contributions are causally linked: diagnosing why selection fails despite strong correlation reveals degeneracy as the binding constraint; QE remains reliable even where selection breaks down, serving as both a practical tool and a diagnostic lens; and the diagnosis directly motivates entity-level construction that succeeds precisely in low-degeneracy regimes.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82).
    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC] 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
    For fine-tuned 4B--8B models, LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.

    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as a diagnostic-motivated mitigation.}
    The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level aggregation, adapting entity voting from ensemble NER \cite{florian2003named} to stochastic sampling: under fine-tuning and zero-shot regimes, LP-weighted construction yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
    Construction and LP selection are complementary on two informative datasets, governed by LP-quality alignment; a simple alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes datasets.
\end{enumerate}

2	
3	Single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.
4	Three factors constrain selection: degeneracy (17.8--67.9\%), limited headroom, and LP compression ($\rho$ 0.043--0.667); within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates with F1 ($\rho{=}0.524$) \cite{eikema2022sampling}.
5	Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), though $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ is post-hoc ($p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.14$; Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}).
6	Temperature disentangles degeneracy from alignment: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve ($\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the selection window narrows with model improvement \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.

8	\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
9	Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms (Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}). \section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

Single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.
Three factors constrain selection: degeneracy (17.8--67.9\%), limited headroom, and LP compression ($\rho$ 0.043--0.667); within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates with F1 ($\rho{=}0.524$) \cite{eikema2022sampling}.
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), though $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ is post-hoc ($p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.14$; Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}).
Temperature disentangles degeneracy from alignment: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve ($\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); the selection window narrows with model improvement \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms (Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}). Degeneracy gates effectiveness: across six FT+ZS combinations, gains are positive when degeneracy ${<}22$\% (FT Few-NERD $13.0$\%, FT SciERC $17.8$\%, ZS SciERC $21.0$\%; all $p{<}0.01$) and absent when ${>}46$\% (ZS Few-NERD, FT/ZS CoNLL). Epoch ablations confirm within-dataset ($11.1{\to}31.3$\% degeneracy halves LP gains; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}). However, under 72B few-shot, construction fails on SciERC ($-0.08$\,pp) despite low degeneracy, indicating that few-shot demonstrations alter the diversity structure in ways that undermine entity-level voting, though the precise mechanism---which is not simple error correlation (Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error})---warrants further study. QE signals remain effective under few-shot (SJ $\rho$ 0.29--0.44), confirming that quality estimation is regime-independent even when construction is not; QE-based selective prediction applies unconditionally, while entity construction should be validated within the target regime.
Alternative strategies (DALS, MBR, DGS) fail to beat greedy (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}); our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding (Appendix~\ref{app:when_selection_works}).

2	
3	Five confidence signals achieve reliable NER quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage). Instance-level selection fails due to degeneracy and LP compression---a structural property that persists at 72B zero-shot scale. Entity-level construction yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC ($p{<}0.005$) under fine-tuning, generalizing to 72B zero-shot where degeneracy is low ($+1.53$\,pp on SciERC), but failing under few-shot where the diversity structure shifts in ways that undermine entity-level voting. For practitioners: use QE for selective prediction; apply construction when multi-sample generation is feasible; assess LP-alignment to route between strategies. 1	Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension} but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
2	All experiments use English-language datasets; cross-lingual generalization remains untested.
3	Entity-level construction assumes the model produces useful partial outputs across samples; when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, 51\% F1${=}0$), this precondition fails and construction cannot improve over greedy.
4	We cover 4B\textendash 8B fine-tuned and 72B zero-shot; the gap persists at 72B but behavior with closed-source APIs or 72B fine-tuning is untested.
5	The 72B zero-shot comparison simultaneously varies model family (Qwen3$\to$Qwen2.5), training regime (fine-tuned$\to$zero-shot), and quantization (FP16$\to$AWQ 4-bit); these factors cannot be fully disentangled.
6	Our supervised approaches (DeBERTa verifier, hidden state probes, MLP/RF on signal combinations) all fail to close the oracle gap; whether content-aware verifiers with access to task-specific structure could succeed remains open.
7	
8	We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
9	The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
10	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
11	LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
12	We tested verbalized confidence \cite{lin2022teaching, tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).
13	Ad-hoc LP${\times}$VC combinations yield at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy (not significant; \S\ref{sec:discussion}); whether \textit{learned} combinations could close the gap remains open.
14	The $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used for tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy.
15	We tested one remedy for LP compression (entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC ($4{\times}$); LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to recover selection (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Our supervised signal combination baseline uses only the five unsupervised signals studied; a DeBERTa verifier encoding input-output pairs also fails to close the gap (preliminary, SciERC $n{=}106$), hidden state probes on the generating model's representations improve correlation ($+37$\% on SciERC) but do not improve selection (gap closure $-5.1$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}), ; the bottleneck extends to model-internal access. Entity embeddings and calibration-based approaches remain untested.
16	Other per-sample scoring methods exist but were not evaluated: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} (consistency of token-level self-evaluation) and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} (model's own probability estimate of correctness) both produce per-sample scores and could in principle address the alignment bottleneck; whether they suffer from similar compression under fine-tuning is unknown.
17	Our selection experiments use 3 training seeds for Few-NERD and CoNLL (stability $\sigma{\leq}0.04$~pp for LP selection); these confirm robustness on the key positive and negative datasets. SciERC uses 1 primary seed with high seed sensitivity ($\sigma{=}0.48$~pp, $n{=}529$), which reflects limited within-seed statistical power.
18	Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs (vs.\ 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence; epoch confound analyses on both Few-NERD (2-point) and SciERC (3-point, including 10-epoch overfitting) are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}.

Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs (vs.\ 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence; epoch confound analyses on both Few-NERD (2-point) and SciERC (3-point, including 10-epoch overfitting) are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} rely on answer-level agreement.
Adaptive variants gate on answer agreement \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive}, input difficulty \cite{wang2025make, feng2025optimal}, or response confidence \cite{kim2026reasc}; \citet{chen2025twofailures} diagnose SC failure modes without proposing gating.
All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different gating signals because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; \citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose two-stage entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction.
LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
Our entity-level construction aggregates across samples from a single fine-tuned model, without requiring model diversity or prompt engineering.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, xie2024selfimproving} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} and self-evaluation guided search \cite{xie2023selfevaluation} learn per-sample scoring.
CISC \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc} and Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derive per-sample confidence from hidden states rather than output statistics, but require architecture-specific access to intermediate representations; these hidden-state signals remain untested for structured prediction (\S Limitations).

256	\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
257	Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
258	For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
259	Structural signals use $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, each additional comparison yields diminishing information.
260	This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
261	For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound (more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate), but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
262	The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

374	\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
375	The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
376	Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to single-sample within a bound $\delta$.
377	The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.

On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, consistent with the NER structural advantage; on full-set RE, however, the SJ--FK difference is non-significant ($\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.005$, $p{=}0.53$; preliminary).
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations: SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$). This holds despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set, where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs, exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

\paragraph{WNUT-17 full signal analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:wnut} reports all five signals on WNUT-17 with full-set and conditional $\rho$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Quality estimation on WNUT-17 (Qwen, $N{=}16$, $T{=}1.0$, $n{=}689$). Cond: non-zero F1 instances ($n{=}334$). Full-set $\rho$ reflects binary success prediction; conditional $\rho$ measures quality gradation. LP's conditional $\rho$ is highest despite negative full-set $\rho$.}
\label{tab:wnut}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Signal & $\rho$ & AUROC & Cond.\ $\rho$ & Cond.\ $p$ \\
\midrule
VC      & .724 & .913 & .038 & .487 \\
FK      & .125 & .555 & .169 & .002 \\
SJ      & .089 & .517 & .288 & ${<}$1e-7 \\
EM      & .050 & .487 & .333 & ${<}$1e-9 \\
LP & $-$.410 & .219 & .350 & ${<}$1e-10 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
The full-set $p$-values are: VC ${<}$1e-112, FK $p{=}0.001$, SJ $p{=}0.020$, EM $p{=}0.194$, LP ${<}$1e-28.
VC's high full-set $\rho{=}0.724$ is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary (conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, $p{=}0.49$), while LP's conditional $\rho{=}0.350$ is the highest among all signals on the non-zero subset, full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.

\paragraph{Cross-configuration selection analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to five additional configurations.
On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of single-sample (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
On LLaMA FewNERD ($n{=}32{,}565$, 3-seed mean), LP is the only signal with positive selection ($+0.36$~pp), confirming LP as the most robust selection signal across model families (Qwen FewNERD: $+1.39$~pp, Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}). All structural signals degrade selection (VC $-2.39$~pp, SJ $-0.52$~pp), consistent with the Qwen pattern. LLaMA FewNERD degeneracy ($23.4{\pm}4.7$\%, 3 seeds) is higher than Qwen ($13.0$\%), illustrating the capability-diversity tension: LLaMA achieves stronger greedy F1 ($0.784$ vs.\ $0.748$, $+3.6$~pp) but at the cost of higher degeneracy ($+10.4$~pp) and reduced oracle headroom ($10.0$ vs.\ $12.4$~pp).
On CoNLL, 48--87\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples; this reflects a ceiling effect (single-sample F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure, and selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Best-of-$N$ selection F1 (macro, instance-averaged) across configurations ($T{=}1.0$, 3-seed mean). Best non-oracle signal per row in \textbf{bold}. LP is the only signal with positive selection on both FewNERD configurations (Qwen $+1.39$~pp, Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}; LLaMA $+0.36$~pp). At $N{=}16$ on LLaMA CoNLL, VC achieves small but significant gains ($+0.28$~pp, $p{<}0.03$; see text below). CoNLL shows especially tight clustering where greedy already exceeds 0.90.}
\label{tab:cross_selection}
\begin{tabular}{llccccccc}
\toprule
Config & $n$ & Greedy & Oracle & SJ & FK & EM & LP & VC \\
\midrule
LLaMA/SciERC $N{=}8$ & 529 & .646 & .778 & .643 & .639 & .634 & \textbf{.652} & .633 \\
LLaMA/SciERC $N{=}16$ & 529 & .645 & .806 & \textbf{.649} & \textbf{.649} & .640 & .646 & .640 \\
\addlinespace
LLaMA/FewNERD $N{=}8$ & 32{,}565 & .784 & .884 & .779 & .779 & .774 & \textbf{.788} & .760 \\
\addlinespace
Qwen/CoNLL $N{=}8$ & 2{,}756 & .908 & .948 & \textbf{.899} & .893 & .898 & .897 & .895 \\
LLaMA/CoNLL $N{=}8$ & 2{,}756 & .924 & .943 & .924 & \textbf{.925} & .924 & .924 & .923 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals use $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, each additional comparison yields diminishing information.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound (more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate), but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
VC achieves the largest gain over single-sample ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions (high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence), signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

\section{Bootstrap CI for Signal Comparisons}\label{app:bootstrap_signal}

Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap_signal_ci} reports bootstrap confidence intervals for individual signal $\rho$ and pairwise $\Delta\rho$ on SciERC NER ($N{=}8$, $n{=}529$, $B{=}10{,}000$, seed${=}42$).
The SJ--LP gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$) is clearly significant, the structural advantage reported in \S\ref{sec:qe_results} is robust.
The VC--SJ gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.019$) is not significant; these two structural signals perform comparably.
The SJ--EM gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.065$) is borderline significant, with the CI lower bound at $+0.003$ and upper bound at $+0.130$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Bootstrap 95\% CIs for signal $\rho$ on SciERC NER ($N{=}8$, $n{=}529$, $B{=}10{,}000$, seed${=}42$). Top: individual signals. Bottom: pairwise $\Delta\rho$; ``Sig.'' indicates whether the 95\% CI excludes zero.}
\label{tab:bootstrap_signal_ci}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Signal & $\rho$ & 95\% CI \\
\midrule
VC & +0.379 & [+0.299, +0.456] \\
SJ & +0.360 & [+0.277, +0.437] \\
EM & +0.295 & [+0.212, +0.371] \\
FK & +0.267 & [+0.176, +0.354] \\
LP & +0.205 & [+0.119, +0.291] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{0.5em}

\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Comparison & $\Delta\rho$ & 95\% CI & Sig. \\
\midrule
SJ $-$ LP & +0.155 & [+0.074, +0.234] & Yes \\
VC $-$ SJ & +0.019 & [$-$0.033, +0.073] & No \\
SJ $-$ EM & +0.065 & [+0.003, +0.130] & Marginal$^\dagger$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\smallskip
{\footnotesize $^\dagger$Marginally significant without multiple comparison correction; would not survive Bonferroni correction for 10 pairwise comparisons ($\alpha_{\text{adj}}{=}0.005$).}
\end{table}

At $N{=}16$ ($B{=}10{,}000$, permutation test), the structural advantage extends to FK comparisons.
On SciERC NER ($n{=}529$), SJ--FK ($\Delta\rho{=}0.147$--$0.160$, all $p{\leq}0.002$) and VC--FK ($\Delta\rho{=}0.138$--$0.188$, all $p{\leq}0.003$) are clearly significant across all three seeds; EM--FK is seed-dependent ($\Delta\rho{=}0.054$--$0.093$, $p{=}0.048$--$0.15$).
On CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), all signals significantly outperform FK: EM $\Delta\rho{=}0.071$ ($p{<}0.001$), SJ $\Delta\rho{=}0.056$ ($p{<}0.001$), VC $\Delta\rho{=}0.022$ ($p{=}0.040$).

\section{Diversity and Selection Analysis}\label{app:diversity}

% fig_selection_gap promoted to main text (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap})

\paragraph{Output diversity quantification.}
Table~\ref{tab:diversity} summarizes output diversity across configurations.
On SciERC, output diversity is substantial: Qwen produces 43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct out of $N{=}8$), with per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.144 and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.
LLaMA shows similar diversity (39\% unique, F1 std 0.11).
On CoNLL, diversity collapses: 59\% (Qwen) to 89\% (LLaMA) of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples; this reflects a ceiling effect where single-sample F1 already exceeds 0.90.
WNUT-17 shows 55\% identical outputs, driven by the 51\% zero-F1 rate.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Output diversity across configurations ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). ``Identical'' = fraction of instances with all $N$ outputs identical. ``Unique'' = mean fraction of distinct outputs per instance.}
\label{tab:diversity}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Config & Identical & Unique \\
\midrule
Qwen/SciERC & 11\% & 43\% \\
LLaMA/SciERC & 18\% & 39\% \\
Qwen/CoNLL & 57\% & --- \\
LLaMA/CoNLL & 88\% & --- \\
WNUT-17 & 55\% & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Oracle-improvable fraction.}
Across SciERC configurations, 39--42\% of instances contain at least one sample with F1 exceeding single-sample\footnote{Oracle-improvable and diversity-stratified analyses use $n{=}529$ (excluding instances with empty gold annotations; see \S\ref{sec:evaluation}); the diversity quantification in Table~\ref{tab:diversity} uses the full test set.}: Qwen NER 42.0\% (222/529, mean headroom $+$31.9~pp among improvable instances), Qwen RE 41.3\% (164/397, $+$45.3~pp), LLaMA NER 39.3\% (208/529, $+$33.7~pp).
On CoNLL, only 4--9\% of instances are improvable, consistent with the ceiling effect.

\paragraph{Diversity-stratified selection gap.}
On the 44\% of Qwen SciERC instances with high diversity (${\geq}4$ unique outputs among 8 samples, $n{=}232$), oracle headroom reaches $+$16.3~pp, yet all consistency-based signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select at or below single-sample, and LP, the only per-sample signal, achieves merely $+$0.8~pp.
LLaMA replicates this pattern: on its high-diversity subset ($n{=}186$), oracle headroom reaches $+$20.1~pp while consistency signals remain at or below single-sample and LP captures only $+$2.0~pp.
This rules out insufficient diversity as an explanation for the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{Instance degeneracy statistics.}
Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy} quantifies instance degeneracy across configurations. ``Constant F1'' denotes instances where all $N$ samples receive identical instance-level F1; ``Constant utility'' denotes instances where MBR (SJ) utility is identical across candidates, preventing ranking.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Instance degeneracy statistics ($T{=}1.0$). ``Constant F1'': all $N$ samples receive identical instance-level F1. ``Constant utility'': MBR (SJ) utility identical across candidates. 4B data confirms degeneracy scales with model capability.}
\label{tab:degeneracy}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
& \shortstack{SciERC 8B\\($N{=}8$)} & \shortstack{SciERC 4B\\($N{=}8$)} & \shortstack{CoNLL 8B\\($N{=}8$)} \\
\midrule
Constant F1 & 17.8\% & 10.4\% & 61.7\% \\
Constant utility & 13\% & 7.0\% & 64\% \\
Oracle gap closed (non-deg.) & 23\% & 25.2\% & 36\% \\
Within-inst.\ SJ $\rho$ (median) & 0.524 & 0.550 & 0.990 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to single-sample within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
These proportions use the same test data that defines the headroom, introducing circularity: $\delta$ is anchored to the very quantity it contextualizes.
We address this below with externally anchored equivalence margins.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$, the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST, ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to single-sample (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\centering
\small
\caption{TOST equivalence testing: signals vs.\ single-sample on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). \checkmark: equivalent at $p{<}0.05$; \texttimes: not equivalent. $\Delta$: mean F1 difference (signal $-$ single-sample).}
\label{tab:tost}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{l cccc cccc}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{NER}} & \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{RE}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-9}
Signal & $\Delta$ & $\pm$2 & $\pm$3 & $\pm$5 & $\Delta$ & $\pm$2 & $\pm$3 & $\pm$5 \\
\midrule
LP & +0.6 & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & $-$0.9 & \texttimes & \checkmark & \checkmark \\
SJ & +0.1 & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & $-$1.8 & \texttimes & \texttimes & \checkmark \\
FK & $-$0.5 & \texttimes & \checkmark & \checkmark & $-$1.6 & \texttimes & \texttimes & \checkmark \\

Yes. All datasets are cited: SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}. Models: Qwen3-8B/4B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct. Training framework: LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory}. Constrained decoding: XGrammar \cite{dong2024xgrammar}. See Sections~\ref{sec:introduction}, \ref{sec:evaluation}, and Appendix~\ref{app:training}.

\item[B2.] \textbf{Did you discuss the license or terms for use and/or distribution of any artifacts?}\\
Partially. The Ethics Statement notes that CoNLL-2003 is derived from the Reuters RCV1 corpus, available under a NIST agreement for research. SciERC, Few-NERD, and WNUT-17 are publicly available research benchmarks. Qwen3 and LLaMA-3.1 are open-weight models released under their respective licenses (Qwen License, Llama 3.1 Community License). Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

\item[B3.] \textbf{Did you discuss if your use of existing artifact(s) was consistent with their intended use?}\\
Yes. All datasets are used for their intended NER evaluation purpose. Models are used for fine-tuning and inference on NER, consistent with their general-purpose design. See Ethics Statement.

\item[B4.] \textbf{Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data contains any information that names or uniquely identifies individual people or offensive content?}\\
N/A. We use established, widely-studied NER benchmarks (news articles, scientific abstracts, social media). No new data was collected or annotated.

\item[B5.] \textbf{Did you provide documentation of the artifacts?}\\
Yes. Dataset domains and characteristics are described in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}. Training configuration details are in Appendix~\ref{app:training}.

\item[B6.] \textbf{Did you report relevant statistics like the number of examples, details of train/test/dev splits, etc.?}\\
Yes. Instance counts are reported in Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd} and throughout Section~\ref{sec:experiments}. Gold-filtering counts, dataset sizes, and evaluation protocol details are in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{C\hspace{0.5em} Did you run computational experiments?}

Yes. See Section~\ref{sec:experiments}.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[C1.] \textbf{Did you report the number of parameters in the models used, the total computational budget, and computing infrastructure used?}\\
Partially. Model sizes (4B, 8B parameters) are stated in Section~\ref{sec:introduction}. LoRA configuration and training hyperparameters are in Appendix~\ref{app:training}. Computing infrastructure: 4$\times$ NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs. We do not report total GPU hours; each model fine-tunes in under 2 hours and inference for $N{=}8$ samples across all test sets completes in under 1 hour per configuration.

\item[C2.] \textbf{Did you discuss the experimental setup, including hyperparameter search and best-found hyperparameter values?}\\
Yes. Appendix~\ref{app:training} (Table~\ref{tab:training}) reports all hyperparameters: LoRA rank/alpha, learning rate, batch size, epochs, optimizer, precision, etc. Both models use identical settings to ensure fair comparison. No extensive hyperparameter search was performed; we use standard LoRA fine-tuning defaults. LoRA rank is ablated in Section~\ref{sec:robustness_main}.

\item[C3.] \textbf{Did you report descriptive statistics about your results?}\\
Yes. We report multi-seed results (3 seeds; $\sigma$ in Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals (Tables~\ref{tab:selection}, \ref{tab:fewnerd_full}), paired bootstrap $p$-values throughout, and minimum detectable effect sizes (Section~\ref{sec:selection_gap}). Tables clearly indicate whether values are single-seed, multi-seed means, or confidence intervals.

\item[C4.] \textbf{If you used existing packages, did you report the implementation, model, and parameter settings used?}\\
Yes. LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} for fine-tuning and XGrammar \cite{dong2024xgrammar} for constrained decoding are cited with version-relevant details in Appendix~\ref{app:training}. Evaluation uses standard span-level micro-F1 (converted to per-instance macro-F1 as described in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{D\hspace{0.5em} Did you use human annotators or research with human subjects?}

No. All experiments use existing annotated benchmarks. No new human annotation or human subjects research was conducted.

\subsection*{E\hspace{0.5em} AI Assistants}

\begin{enumerate}
\item[E1.] \textbf{Did you include information in your paper about your use of AI assistants?}\\
Yes. AI writing assistants were used for drafting and editing. All scientific claims, experimental results, and analyses are the authors' own work, verified against experimental outputs.
\end{enumerate}
